items.title: knowledge_capabilities: server version, protocol version, feature and method lists on the socket (implements #835)
items.description: # Feature Specification: `knowledge_capabilities` — server version, protocol version, feature and method lists on the socket **Feature Branch**: `fabrik/issue-854` **Created**: 2026-11-21 **Status**: Specified **Input**: User description: "Implements #835. ## Problem On the IPC socket, neither `knowledge_health_check` nor `knowledge_status` reports the server version or what the server supports. The version is visible only through `--version` and MCP `initialize`. A raw-socket client can't tell what it's talking to or detect features that shipped after the version it pinned. One integrator, pinned ten minor releases back, built workarounds for methods that already existed. ## Change - Add a new read method, `knowledge_capabilities` (IPC and MCP, read-only, no lock), returning: - `server_version`: the crate version; - `protocol_version`: an integer, starting at 1, bumped on any breaking change to the socket protocol; - `features`: a sorted array of stable feature strings; - `methods`: the sorted list of IPC method names the dispatcher accepts. - Also add `server_version` and `protocol_version` additively to `knowledge_health_check`. - Add a single source of truth for `features` in code (`crates/core/src/capabilities.rs`). Seed it with features that already exist, for example `process_document`, `chunk_supersede`, `walk`, `origin`, `lint`, `writable_groups`, `hybrid_passage_search`. Document in that file and in the ADR that **later issues add their own feature string when they ship**. - Derive `methods` from the dispatcher, not a hand-kept list, or add a test that the two match. - Document it in the IPC reference, and add a CHANGELOG rule to CONTRIBUTING or the release runbook: changes to default scope or response semantics are flagged as breaking for raw-socket clients. ## Acceptance - `knowledge_capabilities` returns a version equal to `CARGO_PKG_VERSION`, protocol 1, and the seeded features and methods. - A test fails if a dispatcher method is missing from `methods`. - The MCP tool count rises by one. Update the tool-count assertions and the docs." ## Background A raw-socket client (for example the Electron app's Python bridge, or a third-party integrator) has no way to ask the running service what it is or what it can do. The server version appears only in `--version` and in the MCP `initialize` response; neither is reachable over the Unix socket / named pipe. items.title: epic: SQLite as the third engine
items.description: SQLite becomes the third engine pbps supports, as a product feature. The maintainer decided this on 2026-11-19, in place of the stub engine that was to be the acceptance of #2798's route step 3. ## Decisions | Question | Decision | |---|---| | Product or test engine | A shipped, supported engine. | | Which engine and library | The C SQLite that applications run, linked through `rusqlite` with its bundled source (3.54.1 today). The library stays behind `pbps-db`'s connection boundary. | | Order of work | An independent `pbps-sqlite` crate first, tested on a real SQLite, with no `Driver` or `Conn` variant and no CLI wiring. It is built alongside #2798's route steps 4 to 6. The wiring comes last, and is those steps' acceptance. | | Table rebuild | May be automatic inside the single apply transaction, behind a new risk class and a hard row cap. | | Version floor | A project field for the minimum SQLite version, default 3.35 (the first with `DROP COLUMN`). The bundled library is at or above it. | ## Why the crate comes before the wiring Adding a `Driver` variant today breaks about 70 exhaustive matches in about 17 existing files, and route steps 4 to 6 are moving every one of them. Arms written by hand now would be thrown away. The crate has no such conflict, and it gives those steps the questions only this engine asks while they are still cheap to answer: no schema namespace, constraints without names, a rebuild as the ordinary path, type affinity, a per-connection `foreign_keys` setting. ## Minimal scope (v0) - Objects: tables; columns with the declared type text, NOT NULL and a literal default; primary key, unique, check, foreign key (with actions); plain, unique and partial indexes; views. - Commands: `pull`, `plan`, `apply`, `state`, `drift`, `baseline`, `bootstrap`. - Changes done in place: create and drop table; add, rename and drop column; create and drop index and view; with a floor that has them, set and drop NOT NULL and add and drop CHECK. - Everything else is refused by name: roles and grants, schemas, sequences, extensions, types, partitions, procedures and functions, the resolver, `pbps test`, `--dev`. After v0: the table rebuild (type, default, key and constraint changes), triggers, generated columns, `WITHOUT ROWID`, `AUTOINCREMENT`, expression indexes, reference data. ## What was measured 34 cases (756 statements) on SQLite 3.46.1 and on 3.54.1 built with the bundled library's own flags, plus locking and identity with file databases and a seco

items.title: GPU stack: pinned image, deploy script and watchdog for reference runs
items.description: Build and debug, without a paid rental, the stack for GPU reference runs: a pinned container image with the official runtime of the candidates (transformers or vLLM with Qwen-Omni support), a deploy script, an independent watchdog with an ownership journal that destroys the instance at the deadline, and a result download with hashes. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] The image tag, its digest and the runtime versions are pinned. The image runs the Gate 0 client on a local CPU smoke without a GPU. - [ ] The deploy script reads the API key only from the local file. It never prints the key and never sends it to the host. - [ ] The watchdog destroys an instance by id at the deadline. It also handles a lost create response. A test with a fake API proves it. - [ ] A dry run against the fake API gives the full timeline: create, ready, weights, smoke, run, download, destroy. - [ ] A document gives the expected deploy time per step with its basis, and marks what only a paid pilot can measure. ## Depends on - Nothing. ## Permissions No rental, no spending. Read-only Vast.ai calls only. ## Technical notes - Earlier pilot (history, not permission): data/corpus/moss-ru-probe-1/vast/ outside git. - Read-only plan in progress: data/corpus/vast-gate0-plan/ outside git.

items.title: [Feature]: Move Downloads from Profile to Library Tab
items.description: ### Area (tag) UI / Layout ### Problem statement The current Desktop layout places Downloads inside the Profile tab. This makes the Profile section serve two different purposes: account/settings management and managing downloaded media. In normal use, downloaded content is something I would expect to access alongside my Library rather than my profile. For example, when I want to watch something I downloaded for offline use, I would naturally look in the Library section first. Having to open Profile to find Downloads makes the navigation less intuitive and makes the Profile tab feel more like a general-purpose storage area instead of a place focused on account and application settings. It would also make the overall navigation more consistent if media-related content stayed together. ### Proposed solution Move the Downloads section from the Profile tab into the Library tab. The Library tab could contain both: The user's library/watchlist content Downloaded content The Profile tab would then primarily focus on: Account/profile information Application settings Preferences Other user or app configuration options Ideally, Downloads could appear as a subsection or clearly separated section within Library, while retaining the existing download functionality. This would make the navigation easier to understand. A user looking for something they have saved or downloaded would have one obvious place to check, while Profile would have a clearer focus on settings and account-related functions. ### Are you planning to implement this yourself? No, this is only a proposal ### Alternatives considered (optional) Keeping Downloads under Profile works functionally, but it is less intuitive because Downloads are media/content rather than profile or account settings. ### Additional context (optional) _No response_

items.title: feat(storefront): show the last price at once, from a cache keyed before the render
items.description: ## Owner's ask (2026-11-22) "We should always show a price. Since we know the last price. It should be cached with the slice. Should be instantly shown." ## Today A price row (`storefront_slice_prices`) is keyed by `price_key`, whose model is the sha256 of the render's 3MF. So the page can read a price only after the render is done: `POST /renders`, then `GET /renders/{job}/estimate`. When the render was pruned (rows past a day) or is new, the visitor waits minutes ("Making your preview and price…") although the same variant was priced before. While a change computes, the page shows no price. ## Change 1. **A variant key known before the render.** `variant_key` = sha256 of the listing id, the listing's published version and the render request's normalized body (what the visitor chose). The visitor's render row keeps it; a `done` price row records it (new column, indexed with `finished_at`; a NEW migration). 2. **An instant read.** `POST /api/store/v1/listings/{id}/price` takes the same body as the render POST and answers at once, with no render and no slice started: - the newest `done` row of the variant key, re-keyed with the shop's settings now (its stored `model_sha256`, the book, the rate, the profile, the printer opening): when that key has a `done` row, `source: "slice"` (firm); - else the newest `done` row's price as `source: "last"` (shown, marked as updating); - else none. 3. **The page never goes blank.** On load and on each change it reads the instant price at the same time as it posts the render. A firm price shows at once. A `last` price, or the price shown before a change, stays on screen with "Updating" until the slice of the render on screen answers, as today. 4. **The charge is unchanged.** A cart line and checkout read `firm_price` by key (`line_prices.py`); the server never takes a price from the browser. ## Not in this issue Warming the cache at publish and "Prepare colours" (scadsy's area, listings and publish).

Where both have one they lie within a metre or two and read as one line; MML adds fences OSM lacks. - 2026-11-21: MML's gates get the plain gate's unmapped mark (#1232's B), with **Access restrictions** from zoom 14 (changed from 16 on 2026-11-21, [#1333](https://github.com/TommiContursi/Polku/issues/1333)'s recommendation 3: they're gates in fences in the countryside, and rare), giving way to OSM's mark where both have one: no second gate symbol, and never red or green, as MML doesn't say who may pass. - 2026-11-21: Ski lifts and cableways are in the basemap, OSM's everywhere and MML's in Finland in one look: a dark line from zoom 13 and a chair along it from 14, the two sources' chairs giving way to each other. Not the Maastokartta's end bars (bars across a line mean no bikes). - 2026-11-21: Masts and chimneys are in the basemap with the Maastokartta's marks from zoom 14, and their height where MML puts it at zooms 14–15. Finland only for now; OSM's beyond Finland is #1318. - 2026-11-21: Dams and breakwaters are in the basemap in the jetties' dark line from zoom 14; beyond Finland in #1318. - 2026-11-21: Transformer stations, other structures and the lifts' pylons are left out. - 2026-11-21: 3D is checked with the build. - From [the choices, round 1](https://github.com/TommiContursi/Polku/issues/1172#issuecomment-7067043485). ## What it would do Show the structures people steer by or stop at in the forest: fences, gates, ski lifts and cableways, dams and breakwaters, masts and chimneys with their heights. ## Where the data is MML's background map (`taustakartta` v21), the `mml` source the map already draws bogs, rock, cliffs, reeds and power lines from (#1160, #1168), with Polku's key or your own. Finland only: MML answers with empty tiles elsewhere. The classes and zooms below come from 67 tiles at Seitseminen, Porvoo, Nuuksio, Nauvo, Koli, Pallas, Kilpisjärvi and a few other places (2026-11-20, zooms 11–14), named from MML's feature catalogue. This problem causes issues since upon a server crash due to some other reason, the variable are set to the values which existed in the previous reboot causing much data loss. ### Steps to Reproduce Save any variable(I used a list -> {eggcount::%player%} ) The variables are not saved to me in the CSV file until the server reboots. items.title: Ask HN: Should Uber Ratings Decay over Time?
items.description: I’ve been thinking about how platforms like Uber calculate reputation scores, and I believe there’s a fundamental flaw in how historical ratings are treated. Uber calculates passenger ratings using the last 500 rated trips, regardless of when those trips occurred. In my case, I have 455 ratings, 426 of which are five stars (93.6%). My overall rating is 4.86. What bothers me isn’t the score itself, but the underlying methodology. A negative rating from five years ago can carry exactly the same weight as one received yesterday. And if you’re an infrequent user who hasn’t accumulated 500 ratings, that negative feedback could influence your reputation for years. This raises an interesting question: Should reputation systems measure your historical average, or should they attempt to represent who you are today? One possible solution is exponential time decay: Weight = 2^(-t/H) Where t is the age of the rating and H is a half-life, perhaps 12 months. Under that approach, a rating from one year ago would carry 50% of its original weight, and one from two years ago just 25%. Of course, this introduces other challenges. How do you prevent someone with a history of poor behaviour from simply waiting for their reputation to recover? How do you maintain statistical confidence for infrequent users? Would Bayesian smoothing or a minimum effective sample size help? There’s also a broader philosophical question around the right to be forgotten. Should digital reputation systems indefinitely preserve the consequences of historical assessments, particularly when those assessments are subjective and potentially no longer representative? I’m curious how others would approach this. * Is a rolling window of 500 ratings statistically defensible without considering time? * Would exponential decay produce a fairer and more predictive reputation score? * Should platforms expose both a lifetime rating and a recent-behaviour rating? * Are there better approaches already being used in other reputation systems? I’d be particularly interested in perspectives from people who’ve worked on marketplace ranking, trust and safety, or reputation algorithms. It seems like a relatively simple mathematical change, but one with potentially significant implications for fairness across digital platforms.

It feels like we all feel threatened by AI, excited by the opportunities, and at the same time, sometimes I feel that as AI has made coding and creation of SaaS companies so competitive that we're also anxious at the same time at the elevated level.

items.description: I wanted to hear some good opinions on all things AI and how they transform the Software industry. I'm anxious about the future and lack the foresight to form any opinion on what to do next. For context, I'm a L4 SWE that has more or less say 5-10 yrs of exp. I've enjoyed my work throughout my career, AI makes me ship more, much more than I could do 3 years ago. I feel I use it well and it translates into really good software. That said, what do you think happens in years to come with the Software industry in general? Do you think we'll go through a massive erosion of jobs? What's your perspective on that? I'm asking because I honestly don't know what to do: I can try to always keep up to date with newest technologies, best practices, but I'm only me; if the demand for SWEs and jobs falls to the floor, I'm not sure I'll always get a place at the table (i.e. land a job) and I'm wondering whether I should try to do something else in some other industry. It feels weird to be in a good position in life and still constantly worry about it getting worse.

items.title: Ask HN: Why no AI-led memory vulns in Python?
items.description: Python usually means CPython, which means C. Most AI-led vulnerabilities lately have been memory mismanagement - what is keeping Python isolated if it is written in C?

items.title: Ask HN: Tips for transitioning from web development to embedded/firmware?
items.description: I started my career 15+ years ago doing native development (c, c++, etc), but the last decade I've been doing fullstack web applications. I'd like to transition closer to my roots with a job doing primarily c, c++ or rust. The natural place seems to be in embedded development or firmware work. How feasible is the transition this late in the game? Any advice?

items.title: Ask HN: When does your app need its own UI vs. using it via MCP?
items.description: I'd love to hear HN user's views on when they think an app their building needs a UI vs just supplies data via MCP to Claude/ChatGPT. If Claude/ChatGPT is where the bulk of work is done in the future (perhaps analogous to a general purpose computer) then how should app developers build in this world?

items.title: Ask HN: Did books that went viral on HN publish their manuscript?
items.description: I'm working on a book that I think is right up HN's alley, but idk if I should publish it in excerpts on Substack like I'm currently doing or just publish the entire manuscript (or rather what I have now) at once.
